content:
Dank cellars are a gold mine for some drinkers. Rather than opening a bottle of wine — or, in some cases, a can of beer — right away, some hobbyists let their alcohol sit on racks for many years to develop complex flavors. And for Americans in particular, one of the most popular collectible beverages is bourbon.

Collecting bottles of the corn-based American whiskey became a common hobby during the so-called “bourbon boom” of the 21st century, but some of the most coveted bottles date back much earlier. And while the boost in sales has waned and the American whiskey category now faces an oversupply, the prices for allocated bourbons keep climbing higher.

This year’s most expensive bourbon, for example, sold for over $10,000 more than last year’s top seller. While the rest of the bourbon industry struggles in the face of low demand, the rising prices for highly allocated bottlings suggests the allure of collectible bourbon shows no signs of slowing down.

From pre-Prohibition whiskeys to special releases, here are the most expensive bourbons in the world right now, according to Wine Searcher.

10. A.H. Hirsch Reserve 17 Year Old Straight Bourbon Whiskey, Pennsylvania, USA

A.H. Hirsch Reserve 17 comes from a historic line of whiskies. In 1974, Adolph Hirsch commissioned a 400-barrel batch of whiskey from a distillery in Schaefferstown, Penn. The whiskies aged untouched for 15 years, until the distillery ceased production in 1989 amid a slump in American whiskey consumption. Hirsch then moved the barrels to Kentucky, where they finished aging and were eventually bottled at 17 years old. The historic lore, coupled with the storied quality of the whiskey, resulted in some of the most coveted bottles of bourbon to date.

  • Average price: $28,801
  • ABV: 47.8%
  • Tasting notes: Toffee, oak, rye spice

9. Old Rip Van Winkle Selection 17 Year Old Pot Stilled Straight Bourbon Whiskey, Kentucky, USA

Casked in 1974 and bottled in 1991 by Julian Van Winkle III, this rare pot stilled Old Rip Van Winkle expression is believed to have been produced at the historic Old Boone Distillery. Originally intended for the Japanese market, this impressive 17-year-old bottling was later released in limited quantities as part of the sought-after Pappy Van Winkle Family Reserve line.

  • Average price: $29,086
  • ABV: 47.8%
  • Tasting notes: Vanilla, dried fruit, aged oak

8. Old Stagg 19 Year Old Straight Bourbon Whiskey, Kentucky, USA

This bourbon from the original George T. Stagg Distillery — now Buffalo Trace — in Frankfort, Ky. was distilled in 1914 and bottled in 1933 as a medicinal whiskey, a unique time capsule of how some distilleries continued production during Prohibition. Buffalo Trace has since revived the Old Stagg label as part of its Prohibition Collection.

  • Average price: $31,746
  • ABV: 50%
  • Tasting notes: Oak funk, rye spice, citrus zest

7. Redemption 36 Year Old Barrel Proof Straight Bourbon Whiskey, USA

Redemption debuted this high-age-statement bourbon as part of its lineup called “The Ancients” in 2017. With just 18 bottles released to the market, this 36-year-old, cask-strength bourbon is one of the most exclusive bottlings out there.

  • Average price: $35,999
  • ABV: 48.8%
  • Tasting notes: Dried citrus, baking spices, smoke

6. Old Rip Van Winkle ‘Van Winkle Special Reserve’ Corti Brothers 19 Year Old Straight Bourbon Whiskey, Kentucky, USA

Produced at the historic Stitzel-Weller Distillery in 1975, this wheated bourbon was distilled specifically for Corti Brothers, a legendary grocery store in Sacramento. When it came time to bottle the whiskey in 1994, Darrell Corti convinced Van Winkle III to package it in a cognac-style decanter.

  • Average price: $35,000
  • ABV: 45.7%
  • Tasting notes: Peach skin, toffee, pepper

5. Old Rip Van Winkle ‘Blue Smoke’ 18 Year Old Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey, Kentucky, USA

Van Winkle III produced this ‘Blue Smoke’ bottling exclusively for Danny Meyer’s New York City barbecue restaurant of the same name in 2003. The origin of this whiskey has never been confirmed, though most collectors and inspectors speculate it came from Stitzel-Weller.

  • Average price: $45,998
  • ABV: 46.3%
  • Tasting notes: Espresso, toasted nuts, oak

4. Old Rip Van Winkle 25 Year Old Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey, Kentucky, USA

Production of this coveted wheated bourbon began in 1989 at the now closed Van Winkle family distillery in Shively, Ky., before Sazerac relocated it to Buffalo Trace in 2002. After 25 years in barrel, the whiskey finished its maturation in stainless steel for three years before bottling. Only 710 bottles of this expression were released.

  • Average price: $46,428
  • ABV: 50%
  • Tasting notes: Oak, dark fruit, chocolate

3. Old Rip Van Winkle ‘Twisted Spoke’ 16 Year Old Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey, Kentucky, USA

The label for Old Rip Van Winkle’s ‘Twisted Spoke’ expression is unlike any other in its lineup. Van Winkle III bottled this whiskey in 1999 for the notorious biker-themed Chicago bar of the same name, which closed in 2025.

  • Average price: $43,628
  • ABV: 52.5%
  • Tasting notes: Oak, cinnamon, cherry, vanilla

2. Old Rip Van Winkle Bottled in Bond Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey, USA

This is an ultra-rare expression of Old Rip Van Winkle’s bottled-in-bond expression produced in 1916 and released in 1934. At the time, the label’s whiskeys were produced in Kentucky before they were aged in a Missouri warehouse and bottled in pint-sized decanters.

  • Average price: $57,301
  • ABV: 50%
  • Tasting notes: Caramel, vanilla, dark fruit

1. Society of Bourbon Connoisseurs 20 Year Old Cask Proof Bourbon Whiskey, Kentucky, USA

If you thought the most expensive bourbon had nothing to do with the Van Winkle name, think again. There is no Society of Bourbon Connoisseurs — Van Winkle III created the lofty title specifically for this label of 20-year-old cask strength bourbons he produced for the Japanese market.

  • Average price: $64,356
  • ABV: 53.5%
  • Tasting notes: Molasses, toffee, nuts, dried fruit

title: We Asked 15 Bartenders: What’s Your Go-To Tailgating Drink?
summary:
Tailgating is a traditional game day staple for many. It’s also the one moment of guaranteed Sunday afternoon happiness. For some football fans, it represents the initial spark of joy that gradually transforms into the afterglow of their favorite team’s triumph. For others, it’s the last bastion of glee before a frustrating loss. Win or lose, though, the tailgate’s bevy of food and beverage enjoyed in revelry among good friends never ceases to delight. There is only one real rule to a tailgate: Have a good time.

The article We Asked 15 Bartenders: What’s Your Go-To Tailgating Drink? appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Tailgating is a traditional game day staple for many. It’s also the one moment of guaranteed Sunday afternoon happiness. For some football fans, it represents the initial spark of joy that gradually transforms into the afterglow of their favorite team’s triumph. For others, it’s the last bastion of glee before a frustrating loss. Win or lose, though, the tailgate’s bevy of food and beverage enjoyed in revelry among good friends never ceases to delight.

There is only one real rule to a tailgate: Have a good time. This simple mandate leaves what one chooses for their tailgating drink of choice to be completely open to interpretation. It may be something as basic as a crisp beer or as fancy as a pinkies-out cocktail. As long as the imbiber acts responsible, there are no wrong answers.

For bartenders, a Sunday tailgate can be a great way to unwind after back-to-back Friday and Saturday nights. It may take some effort to get out of the house, but the opportunity to be immersed in the unique social culture of the NFL tailgate with their beverage of choice makes overcoming the struggle worthwhile. With that in mind, we asked 15 bartenders about the one drink they tend to reach for most often when they tailgate prior to kickoff. In quite a few cases, supporting the local pro team also means throwing their support behind local products.

The go-to tailgating drinks for bartenders:

  • Miller Lite & Jameson Irish Whiskey
  • Rainier Beer
  • Monday Night Brewing 404 Lager and ASW Fiddler Wheated Bourbon
  • Michelada
  • Bloody Mary
  • Spicy Ranch Water
  • Huss Brewing Co. Devil’s Halo Lager
  • Freezer Door Old Fashioned
  • Sierra Nevada Pale Ale
  • Georgia Peach Mule
  • Suntory Toki Whisky Highball
  • Second District Brewing Co. Bancroft Beer and shot of Old Grand-Dad Bottled in Bond
  • Labatt Blue Light
  • Bubbly
  • Dibon Cava
  • Ranch Water
  • High Noon
  • Red Snapper

“Football calls for beer and whiskey, and when you have tickets to an NFL game and a tailgating opportunity, it’s a perfect pairing. However, It is important to consider the amount of time you will be consuming drinks, so you want to have a long-term plan. I personally like to stick to a lower ABV beer that is crisp and light if I plan to drink the whole day, and Miller Lite is perfect for the job. It also tastes delicious straight from a can, the preferred packaging in a parking lot. It can get really cold here in Chicago, and on these occasions, you need to supplement your beverage choice with something that will warm you up, like whiskey. My personal favorite is Jameson Irish Whiskey. It is straightforward, has a kick to remind you that you’re drinking whiskey, and warms you from the inside.” —Sarah Clark, director of operations and beverage director, The Dearborn, Chicago

“My go-to tailgating drink is Rainier Beer. As a transplant who’s called Seattle home for the past 12 years, Rainier has become the perfect bridge between where I came from and where I am now. I still miss cracking open a Yuengling back East and the nostalgia of PBR and Camel Lights outside my favorite dive bar, but Rainier has earned its place in the cooler on game day. It’s approachable, unpretentious, and deeply tied to the Pacific Northwest. Whether I’m watching my favorite NFL team or gathering with friends before kickoff, Rainier is the beer I reach for every time.” —Emelio Sansone, executive chef, Tin Lizzie Lounge, Seattle

“We love our Sundays and a full day of football, but when it comes to camaraderie and pride, nothing beats Monday Night Football. One game, one party, all eyes on the same ball. For that, only local beverages will do. There are two local Atlanta companies which reflect the hard work and passion that flow throughout the city: Fiddler Wheated Bourbon and 404 Lager from Monday Night Brewing. Fiddler has a rich history and delivers a spicy finish, and if you see me with an ice-cold 404, you’ll likely find me wearing a subtle smile and feeling perfectly content.” —William Cutting, F&B specialist, Hartley Kitchen and Cocktails, Atlanta

“I love tailgating. I’m not a sports guy though, so to me tailgating is reminiscent of a more chaotic brunch. This means it’s perfect for morning beverages, so I will want a spicy Michelada or Bloody Mary. If you’re going to support a local team, you need to also support local brands, so I’m using Threes Brewing Echo of Nothing for my Michelada. For my Bloody Mary, I’m using Sinpatch vodka by Tenmile Distilling.” —Atticus Bashore, head bartender, Chambers, New York City

“It’s Texas, so of course tailgaters want a Ranch Water. As football season arrives in Houston, fans are searching for a refreshing, palate-pleasing libation, and a Ranch Water — specifically, a Spicy Ranch Water — is an easy, build-on-the-spot cocktail anyone can make. With minimal prep — all you need to do is just pre-slice jalapeños and juice fresh lime — tailgaters can stay focused on the BBQ. The jalapeño adds subtle spice without reading as heavy throughout the day. Non-tequila drinkers can omit the tequila for a spirit-free version, providing three crowd-pleasing options to cheer on the Texans.” —Andrea Johns, bar lead, The Naturalist Bar & Lounge, Houston

“In 2024, Huss Brewing Co. announced a partnership with ASU (Arizona State University) to brew Devil’s Halo Lager, the official craft beer of Sun Devils Athletics. Each sale will benefit the Sun Angel Collective, which helps fund and broker Name, Image, and Likeness (NIL) deals for ASU student athletes. On Sundays, we’re drinking Devil’s Halo while we’re watching the Cardinals, but we are supporting our local University while also championing those who are trying to reach the ultimate stage in football.” —Ashley Traynor, F&B operations manager, The Phonecian Tavern, Scottsdale, Ariz.

“On those cold fall and winter mornings when you can barely feel your fingers, you need something a little stronger than a beer to keep you warm. What I like to drink in those situations is a freezer door Old Fashioned. You batch the cocktail at home with the bourbon, bitters, and syrup, then add water for dilution. No need to stir or bring any tools to the tailgate. Just pour, enjoy, and root for your team!” —Nick Kanakaris, general manager and beverage director, Aubrey’s Corner, Summit, N.J.

“My go-to tailgating drink would be Sierra Nevada Pale Ale. My husband is a huge football fan, and my first real experience watching football with him involved a Sierra Nevada Pale Ale, so the two have been connected in my mind ever since. It’s also become one of my go-to outdoorsy beers. I spend so much of my professional life thinking about wine — quality, flavor profiles, pairings, etc. — that sometimes it’s nice to just open a beer and enjoy it without analyzing anything. And Sierra Nevada’s bitterness is exactly what I want, especially with jalapeño poppers.” —Kinga Mackowiak, beverage director, Apple Blossom, Denver

“My go-to tailgating drink is a Georgia Peach Mule, made with bourbon, spicy roasted peach purée, fresh muddled lime, agave nectar, and Fever-Tree Ginger Beer. It has everything I want for game day: It’s cold and refreshing, with some heat from the roasted peaches and just enough sweetness to balance the bourbon and lime. It also feels distinctly Georgian without becoming overly complicated. The ingredients can be batched ahead of time, then topped with ginger beer when everyone is ready for a drink, so it’s easy to serve to a group without spending the entire tailgate mixing cocktails.” —Damien McGee, owner, Vesper, Atlanta

“Our go-to tailgating drink would be a Suntory Toki Japanese Whisky Highball. For tailgating, I like something refreshing, simple, and easy to enjoy with food, and a Toki Highball checks all of those boxes. The whisky’s light, crisp character with plenty of cold soda makes it refreshing without overpowering the food, especially grilled meats and barbecue. It’s also easy to make and serve, which is exactly what you want when you’re tailgating.” —Tana Kokanot, head bartender, Jeong Yuk Jeom, NYC

“In South Philly, there are few things we love more than a Citywide Special: Philadelphia’s pairing of an affordable beer and a shot of whiskey. Whether you’re watching from your favorite bar or in the Birds’ parking lot, for me, a pint of Bancroft Beer from Second District Brewing alongside a shot of Old Grand-Dad Bottled in Bond always kicks off an Eagles game in good fashion. Go Birds!” —Chris Liu, beverage director, Bloomsday, Philadelphia

“Living in the city of Buffalo and being a Bills fan, I have grown up drinking Labatt Blue Light at almost every tailgate I have ever been to. It’s crisp, classic, reliable, and low ABV enough that you will become full before you’ve drunk enough to make a complete fool of yourself. Another beautiful thing about football is the 1 p.m. Sunday start time, which means arriving at the stadium before 9 a.m. If you are starting that early, the only alternative to beer to drink that early in the morning is bubbly. Prosecco or Cava made into something fun and delicious; preferably a spritz with a little soda water to keep it lower in alcohol content. My favorite Cava right now is Dibon — it’s super delicious and high quality for the price point and makes a phenomenal spritz.” —Mary Bennett, bar manager, Mira, Buffalo

“My vote is a Ranch Water: grab a Topo Chico in a glass bottle, open it, drink some, then add a quality blanco tequila and a slice of lime. I’ve been digging the Cascahuín Tahona Blanco. The great thing about this method is that you control your own ratio as the day goes on, and if you want to skip a few rounds, no one notices. It’s built for a day full of tailgating.” —Justin Ware, operations director, Johnny’s Gold Brick, Houston

“My go-to tailgate drink is a High Noon. I’m definitely a seltzer girly, especially on game day, because I want something light and refreshing that won’t leave me feeling weighed down. Tailgating in Detroit can easily become an all day event, so I like something I can sip while comfortably pacing myself while cheering on the Lions.” —Tara Wong, beverage manager, Gilly’s Clubhouse, Detroit

“I love a Red Snapper made with Dorothy Parker New York Gin for tailgating (and pretty much any other Sunday occasion). The gentle fruit and florality of the gin pair really nicely with the spice and acidity of the tomato, citrus, Worcestershire, and hot sauce, making it particularly sessionable. It’s also ideal for a New York tailgate because it’s just as delicious batched into a pitcher and poured into Solo cups as it is made one at a time. Add a celery stick, an olive, and, if you’re peckish, a cooked shrimp, and you’re set for game day.” —Jamie Gordon, bar and creative director, Jaywalker, NYC

content:
Describe a wine as buttery, and most picture Chardonnay. Some might even turn up their nose, having written off the variety entirely as rich, oaky, or creamy without realizing that those characteristics often come from winemaking decisions — not the grape itself — and represent just one example of the variety’s potential. In fact, Chardonnay is anything but one-dimensional.

“One of the things that makes Chardonnay such an exciting grape is its versatility and range of styles. You have everything from crisp, minerally Chablis to flinty oaked Meursault to stereotypical butter bombs,” says Greg Stokes, owner of Columbus, Ohio’s Cordial Cocktail Club and bottle shop. In Burgundy alone, the grape’s birthplace, Chardonnay can range from fresh, fruit-forward wines meant to be enjoyed young to fuller, more textured styles with riper fruit, including some of the world’s most prized, age-worthy examples.

Winemakers also love the grape for its adaptability and how well it responds to different winemaking techniques, like oak aging, malolactic fermentation, and time on the lees. Each yields different flavors and textures, offering plenty of room to experiment.

Once you identify what you like about Chardonnay, it’s worth seeing what else is out there. With over 10,000 known grape varieties, plenty showcase some of the same qualities that make Chardonnay one of the world’s most widely planted grape varieties — and many at a fraction of the cost. Here are nine to seek out on your next trip to the grocery store or wine bar.

Aligoté

Often playing second fiddle to Burgundy’s prized Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, the grape has grown in popularity the last few decades for its relative affordability. Some of the region’s most respected producers make Aligoté alongside their more prestigious — and often much pricier — wines. “Aligoté wines are bright and full of zesty citrus, smoke, and light herbal notes,” Derek Mizell, wine lead at Only the Wild Ones in Austin says. Mizell suggests trying producers like Sylvain Pataille or Alice et Olivier de Moor.

Chenin Blanc

Known for its high acidity and versatility, Chenin Blanc grows in cool, moderate, and warm climates and can take on a broad range of styles, from sparkling and dry to sweet and age-worthy. And while the grape hails from the Loire Valley, its popularity in South Africa — where it’s also known as Steen — has exploded, making the country one of the world’s largest producers. “If you love a rich, buttery Chardonnay, try a barrel-aged Chenin from South Africa, or if you prefer a crisp, unoaked version, look for Vouvray in the Loire Valley,” Aaron Walker, director of winemaking operations at California’s Pali Wine Co suggests.

Viognier

Like Chardonnay, Viognier is anything but shy. While both tend to have a luxurious texture, the Northern Rhône grape is often fuller-bodied and more aromatic than Chardonnay. “If you like Chardonnay for its fruitiness while having that round texture and fuller body, Viognier is a great alternative because it has all the same characteristics, just with slightly different fruit flavors,” says Wade Hill, sommelier at Lautrec in Pennsylvania. While beautiful examples exist in its native France, Viognier from Virginia and Southern Australia are also exciting places to seek out.

Sémillon

If you love a crisp Chardonnay but also appreciate what a little bottle age can do, Sémillon offers solid value in either style. Young examples are bright and zippy, with flavors of lemon and green apple, while bottle-aged wines develop richer, more complex flavors of honey, toast, and beeswax. Native to Bordeaux, where it plays a role in both dry and sweet wines, Australia (particularly the Hunter Valley) has found success with dry, single-variety Sémillon. Try Adega Vinho’s 2023 Sémillon Reserve, or look for an older Hunter Valley bottling.

Marsanne

Marsanne is best known for its role in the celebrated white wines from Hermitage, where it’s often blended with Roussanne. Bottled on its own, expect a full-bodied, deliciously textured wine, with notes of pear and stone fruit, or as it ages, almond and honey. For Braith Gill, beverage director at Brennan’s in New Orleans, those who love Chardonnay for its texture should try Marsanne. Outside the Rhône, some beautiful examples come from warmer climates like California, Texas, and Australia. Try Uplift Vineyard’s 2024 Marsanne from Texas Hill Country, which absolutely sings.

Grenache Blanc

A white-skinned mutation of Grenache Noir, Grenache Blanc is a full-bodied white grape with roots in Spain and a long history in France. The grape can show pear, white peach, and melon, along with floral or herbal notes and a plush palate. Look to Spain’s Terra Alta for fresher, mineral-driven styles, or Spain’s Priorat and France’s Southern Rhône for bolder expressions. “You get those green and golden apple notes, along with a broad, rounded mouthfeel that can remind you of a Chardonnay that has gone through malolactic fermentation,” says Fah Sathirapongsasuti, sommelier, winemaker, and co-owner at California’s Sunset Cellars.

Garganega

Say that 10 times fast. The indigenous grape behind most Soave wines in Italy’s Veneto region, Garganega can range from lean and crisp to richer, nuttier styles, often with notes of citrus, stone fruit, and almond. Its range is part of what makes it a solid alternative to Chardonnay, particularly for those who value punchy acidity and some texture but want something light on its feet. For a classic expression, try Pieropan Soave Classico 2023, or, to taste the grape’s more decadent side, grab a bottle of Pasqua Romeo and Juliet Passimento Bianco 2024.

Godello

For the Chard fan with a soft spot for Burgundy, look west to Spain. “The body and fruity profile of Godello is very similar to French Chardonnay,” Stokes says. “The younger styles like Emilio Moro ‘Polvorete’ or Alberto Orte ‘A Portelo’ are perfect for the Chablis drinker, while bottles with more oak aging like Emilio Moro’s ‘La Revelía’ or Alberto Orte’s ‘Escalada Do Sil’ readily scratch an itch for those who crave Côte d’Or Burgundies,” says Stokes. Also search for bottles from Valdeorras, the grape’s signature region in Galicia.

Xarel-lo

Just as Chardonnay is a key grape in making Champagne, Xarel-lo helps give Cava its signature style, bringing structure, acidity, and sea-salt minerality to Spain’s beloved sparkling wine. Bottled on its own as a still wine, the Catalan grape can yield lively, textured wines with notes of stone fruit, citrus, and spice. With time on the lees, it develops greater depth, creaminess, and aromatic complexity while retaining its Mediterranean quality. Check out bottles from Penedès-based producers like Anima Mundi or Enric Soler.

content:
The newest trick (and treat) from E&J Gallo’s Apothic Wine is a bloody bag of red wine.

Ahead of October, the brand known for inky red blends partnered with queen of Halloween Heidi Klum on a package designed to resemble a blood transfusion bag. Apothic Type ‘A’ Blood Bag dropped online in limited numbers at 10:31 p.m. Thursday night.

The newest campaign from Gallo — which is the largest wine supplier in the U.S. and is driving the alternative packaging movement with innovations like TetraPaks — is an attempt at segueing its product into “adult party spaces,” Gallo’s vice president of power and ascending brands, Marshall Dawson, says.

“This is not a limited-time-offer of a different product,” Dawson says. “It’s a usage vehicle that connects with the idea that is fun, different, and occasion based.”

A purchase of Apothic Type ‘A’ Blood Bag comes as two, empty bags in a soft, red cooler for $10.31. Gallo formatted the release as a limited-time drop with hints at a possible second round of purchases opening later this month — a relatively new format within the broader wine industry that garners hype and intrigue.

Part of the Apothic and Klum collab is a chance for one fan and a guest to attend Klum’s megawatt Halloween party this year. With its black-and-red, gothic branding, Apothic has long associated itself with Halloween, but the partnership with Klum — who is known for showstopping costumes and hosting an annual, star-studded party — is a move to both boost Apothic’s presence during an already-lucrative season and expand to new consumers.

“Halloween has grown in the past few decades with billions of dollars,” Dawson says. “And there is an overlap in the Millennial to younger-Gen X audience, which I would call our core consumer and the same for Heidi. But because of her staying power and because of her scale, it’s a beautiful marketing program that helps us with our current consumer with a side opportunity to recruit new consumers.”

The non-breakable, resealable bags come as Apothic — whose flagship blend combines Zinfandel, Syrah, and Merlot, among other red grapes — releases 200-milliliter TetraPak cartons to markets, a move that Dawson envisions will recruit new drinkers.

Dawson already sees upticks in sales and brand engagement after announcing the collaboration on Tuesday.

“I can tell you right now: It’s working,” he says.

content:
This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on Scottish distillers’ responses to a new English single malt category, Trump to lift Irish whiskey tariff, the latest product releases, and more.

News to know:

  • New English single malt designation riles up Scots: Scottish distillers are furious after the British government designated English single malt as a distinct whisky category. Scottish distillers are lobbying against the new protected status and arguing that the criteria for English single malts are looser than those for Scotch: To earn the premium designation, Scotch distillers must produce single malts entirely onsite, whereas the English distinction allows for some steps to be completed at separate locations. The Scottish Whisky Association plans to discuss the matter this week with British government officials.
  • Some better news in across-the-pond whiskey: President Donald Trump said he plans to lift the 10 percent tariff on Irish whiskey earlier this week. Trump, who wedged his announcement into the trophy ceremony for the Irish Open, said “everybody’s been bugging” him to drop the levy, professional golfers included.
  • Sazerac continues its buying spree: Just days after finalizing its reportedly £300 million ($405 million) purchase of U.K. brand Au Vodka, Sazerac is now in talks to acquire German schnapps producer Berentzen-Gruppe AG, Bloomberg reports. It’s the latest development in the Louisville, Ky.-based spirits producer’s 2026 shopping spree: Earlier this year, Sazerac shuffled a $15 billion offer to buy out competitor Brown-Forman.
  • Summit Brewing defaults on $8.2 million loan: One of the country’s largest craft breweries faces foreclosure by its lender. BMO Bank, the secured lender for the St. Paul, Minn.-based brewery, initiated foreclosure activities last week, as first reported by The Minnesota Star-Tribune. Once the state’s largest craft brewery, Summit has struggled in recent years with the overall downturn in craft beer. From 2022 to 2023 alone, its volume output plummeted by over 30 percent, according to Brewbound.

Product releases to watch:

  • Apothic goes gory with “bloody” wine bags: E&J Gallo’s Apothic Wine partnered with Halloween queen Heidi Klum on a seasonally inspired bag of wine made to resemble a blood transfusion bag. Apothic Type ‘A’ Blood Bag will be available online as a limited-drop release for a suggested retail price of $10.31 for two bags.
  • Knob Creek unveils 12-year-old bourbon: James B. Beam Distilling Co.-owned Knob Creek debuted 12 Year Old Cask Strength on Wednesday. The high-proof whisky, bottled at 121.2 proof, will be available nationwide for a limited time at a suggested retail price of $89.99.
  • The Macallan launches third release in TIME : SPACE Collection: The cult brand added a 20-year-old Scotch finished in sherry casks to its ultra-premium lineup. The Macallan TIME : SPACE Sherry Cask, bottled at 44.8 percent ABV, is available for purchase through the distillery’s lottery system for $1,400.

title: Rare Beer Was Once a Collector’s Dream. Now, It’s a Liability.
summary:
A group of former hipsters sit around a San Francisco apartment in bow ties, newsboy caps, and suspenders. They listen to 2012 indie folk music. Someone jokingly calls it a “lost ‘Portlandia’ episode.” The group has gathered — in the present day, mind you — to drink craft beers from the previous decade. A 2015 bottle of Firestone Walker Stickee Monkee, a barrel-aged quadruple from California. A Scarface Imperial Stout from Speakeasy Ales & Lagers.

The article Rare Beer Was Once a Collector’s Dream. Now, It’s a Liability. appeared first on VinePair.
content:
A group of former hipsters sit around a San Francisco apartment in bow ties, newsboy caps, and suspenders. They listen to 2012 indie folk music. Someone jokingly calls it a “lost ‘Portlandia’ episode.”

The group has gathered — in the present day, mind you — to drink craft beers from the previous decade.

A 2015 bottle of Firestone Walker Stickee Monkee, a barrel-aged quadruple from California. A Scarface Imperial Stout from Speakeasy Ales & Lagers. A 14-year-old De Struise Brouwers Black Albert, a Russian imperial stout (from Belgium) once considered one of the finest beers in the world around the time it was purchased.

This gathering is what the host, Wes Leslie, calls an “expired craft beer party.”

In the early-2010s, he had begun collecting barrel-aged beers, buying rare releases when he worked at Speakeasy, grabbing other cool bottles he saw when he hit specialty beer stores in town, like the famed (and now closed) City Beer Store in San Francisco.

“I just thought it’d be like fun to have a little cellar,” Leslie tells me. And by “cellar,” he meant some bottles tucked under his bar. “Then the years passed and I just sort of fell out of love with beer. I became more of a cocktail guy. Then it was just like, I’ve sat on them so long, I don’t even like beer anymore.”

Thus, the expired craft beer party where Leslie and several other friends — many former craft beer nuts themselves who had fondly enjoyed the beers when they were fresh in the previous era — tasted through a few dozen over-aged bottles.

Though Leslie found all the beers still interesting, and some better than others, he ultimately agreed they had aged way too long and were now “kinda disgusting.”

At least they were no longer in his life.

Cellaring or Hoarding?

I, too, bought and cellared way too much beer during the last decade.

Cases and cases of Goose Island Bourbon County Brand Stout and its many variants. Wax-dipped bombers of Three Floyds Dark Lord that I actually acquired at Dark Lord Day in Indiana back in 2010. Countless stouts from breweries like Hardywood Park, Founders, and Side Project and wild ales from breweries like The Rare Barrel, Jester King, and de Garde. I still have a full vertical of The Bruery’s 12 Days of Christmas, a series I began collecting in 2008 with the release of Partridge in a Pear Tree and ended seven years ago with the release of 12 Drummers Drumming.

When did this “cellaring” — this hoarding — begin?

I began drinking craft beer casually in college, back when fruit beers like Sam Adams Cherry Wheat, Abita Purple Haze, and Magic Hat #9 signaled something other than the ubiquitous macro swill. After I moved to New York, in the nascent days of the city’s craft beer scene, I bought 6-packs of whatever quality stuff I could find — Brooklyn Lager, Victory HopDevil, Belgian imports like Duvel — and fully consumed it before the weekend was over. But by the late aughts, distribution was improving and I was getting obsessive. I found Beer Advocate’s Top 100 Beers in the World and set out to taste them all.

Russian River’s Pliny the Elder and Younger, Portsmouth Brewing Kate The Great, Founders Kentucky Breakfast Stout, the aforementioned Black Albert.

These were limited beers you sometimes had to travel the country to find, high-ABV beers released perhaps once per year, beers you had to go to specific spots in Europe to nab, like the longtime “#1 beer in the world” Westvleteren XII, a Trappist quadruple released almost exclusively from the monastery and so rustic in appearance it literally didn’t even have a label.

These were still my broke and single days, which meant I was constantly moving apartments throughout the five boroughs and, thus, the idea of cellaring beers was mostly an impossibility. Still, I slowly started setting a few choice ones aside — Firestone Walker Parabola, The Bruery Black Tuesday, Surly Darkness — whenever I got more than one bottle of them. The stash moved with me each time, not to a cellar but to a closet floor, the back of a pantry, sometimes the bookshelf, wedged in beside whatever I was reading that year.

That changed when I moved in with the woman who’d become my wife in 2012. Suddenly I had roots, a multi-room apartment with no roommates (besides her), and somewhere permanent to put beer. She’d taken me for a minimalist — a couple suitcases of clothes, a few boxes of books, not a stick of furniture. She’d soon learn I was just waiting for space.

Craft beer was hitting a fever pitch by then, with events and rare releases and festivals nearly every weekend, and I was finally making a little money. So when I came upon cases of Goose Island Bourbon County Rare — their famed imperial stout aged, for the first time, in 23-year-old Pappy Van Winkle barrels — at a Whole Foods in 2010, I could afford several bottles even at $45 a pop. When I hit a release of The Lost Abbey’s Duck Duck Gooze in Southern California, I muled an entire case home. And when we traveled to Belgium in 2013, I jammed as many bottles of Cantillon into my luggage as I could legally get back to America without lying to customs.

Yes, I was drinking plenty of these beers over the years — god, I still wish I had some of that Duck Duck Gooze — but I was cellaring even more.

And then, like Leslie, somewhere around the start of the Covid-19 pandemic, I kind of fell out of love with beer.

The Regret

“There is not a day that goes by that I do not regret my ridiculous collection,” says Christopher Nyren, referring to his complete set of every Goose Island “big” beer (stouts, barleywine, strong ales) ever released, even bootlegs.

The 48-year-old Chicago man started cellaring beer in 2014, as the hobby was peaking: hazy IPAs traded across the country weekly, pastry stouts flipped online the day they dropped, and, as Nyren puts it, “rare lambics selling like vintage Bordeaux.” His cellar once topped 500 bottles; he’s since winnowed it to around 350, mostly centered on Revolution’s Deep Wood barleywine cans and 88 bottles of rare lambic — among them a birth-year 1977 Cantillon and a jeroboam of Bokke Framboos — kept in a walk-in wine fridge he built inside the sub-basement nuclear bomb shelter he uses as a cellar (seriously).

“They’ve all passed their prime, and at this point you might as well just crack them.”

By his own count he’s spent $12,500 on the beer currently down there, and he knows he couldn’t get half that for it now, because nobody buys secondary-market beer anymore. Likewise, he laments it’s gotten quite hard to get beer nerds together for bottle shares or themed verticals, no matter how high-caliber the offerings.

“Nowadays, it’s hard to even give away your beer,” says Nyren.

He would know, as he’s spent real effort helping friends purge their own hoards, including one sitting on hundreds of bottles from Pips Meadery — once the top-rated producer on all of Untappd — who just wanted them gone. “He was less price sensitive and more focused on speed to close,” Nyren says. With the meads, he fears he’ll never find a single buyer at all.

The lament is everywhere. On the forums and private Facebook groups once used to buy, sell, and trade these bottles, collectors now post about cellars they can’t unload. One recent thread was titled “A Nightmare on Cellar Street.”

My friend and fellow booze scribe Brad Japhe has an immense cellar too, including, like me and Nyren, tons of old bottles of Bourbon County Brand Stout. He jokes that no one he knows would be impressed anymore if he uncorked a 2013 Proprietor’s, a Chicago-only release that once sold for hundreds.

He did find one good way to draw down the stash. A diehard Knicks fan, Japhe booked a hotel room on the team’s championship parade route in June and invited friends up to drink through once-ballyhooed bottles, including a 12-year-old Russian River Consecration. It was still tasty, but showed him the folly in having sat on it so long.

“Guess what, it didn’t really taste at all better than any Consecration you’d just pluck from the shelf in 2026,” he told me. “So maybe we were oversold on the idea of cellaring being so worthwhile with wild ales.”

Indeed, back in the 2010s, the case for cellaring was everywhere from magazine features to endless message-board threads.

“One of the hottest trends right now is aging craft beer,” wrote Patrick Dawson, author of “Vintage Beer: A Taster’s Guide to Brews That Improve Over Time,” in a piece for The Denver Post back in 2015. His advice, at the time, was to age beers from the “S” categories: strong, sour, or smoked. Barleywines, stouts, Belgian strong ales, lambics, Flanders reds — or pretty much everything in my cellar.

At the time, Dawson had over 200 beers, with some dating back to 1972.

“For the most part with those beers, it’s more just fun to open a beer that old,” he said. “It’s pretty unusual for one of those to actually be a really enjoyable experience to drink. More often than not, they are just going to be more muted with not a lot of flavor.”

Crack ’Em

Early on in the pandemic, my family moved to bigger digs and since 2020 I’ve had, for the first time, an actual cellar, a low-ceilinged room in our Brooklyn apartment where my head nearly scrapes the exposed pipes. We store our tools there, extra lightbulbs, the ski gear, holiday decorations…and the hundreds of “rare” beers I spent tens of thousands of dollars on back in the late aughts and 2010s.

Now, whenever I head down for the power drill or to grab a suitcase before a trip, I’m met by this wall of beer, confronted by the follies of my past.

Deschutes The Abyss, Kuhnhenn Fourth Dementia, Bell’s Black Note, Hunahpu’s Imperial Stout (the ultra-rare apple brandy version no less!), boxes upon boxes of Firestone Walker Anniversary.

All caked in dust.

I’m 47 now and I mostly drink spirits and cocktails. I still drink beer, but I don’t fetishize it, and I certainly don’t collect it. I buy pilsners and lagers and the occasional IPA, and they go in the fridge and get drunk within days, the same way I drank beer at 22. Meanwhile the cellar holds boxes of coffee-infused imperial stouts and 18 percent barleywines and wax-dipped pastry stouts in 750-mL bottles, each one surely a night-long project that would leave me bloated and overwhelmed by acid reflux for days.

“There is not a day that goes by that I do not regret my ridiculous collection.”

I was saving these beers for some special occasion. But plenty of special occasions came and went and I never drank them.

And there they sit: too worthless now to sell, too heavy to haul upstairs on a whim, too fraught to simply throw away because tossing them would mean admitting my wife was right a decade ago, when she kept asking why I needed to buy more beer when I already had so much.

I only had one choice, and Leslie’s advice kept ringing in my head:

“They’ve all passed their prime, and at this point you might as well just crack them.”

The Uncellaring

And so I did, almost nightly for a month straight.

The first chance came on our 12th wedding anniversary. As it happened, I’d cellared a few of the beers we’d actually served at the wedding, including a 2014 The Bruery Mischief, a Belgian-style golden ale we’d both loved.

The bottlecap came off with a sad little wheeze — not promising. I poured us each a wine glass anyway. Flat and flabby, the hops were long gone, and whatever brightness it once had faded to a dull, oxidized maltiness. It was…not good. We poured roughly 730 of the 750 mL bottle down the sink. Happy anniversary, honey. At least the cellar was one bottle smaller.

Next up was a 2015 Russian River Sanctification, their sublime wild ale aged in Pinot Noir barrels with cherries added. Also flat, also a disappointment. As was the Jester King SPON 2016 Méthode Gueuze, once one of the greatest American beers of all time.

But they weren’t all duds. A 2017 Bourbon County Coffee had held up beautifully, its coffee turned to a rich, milk-chocolate mocha — this despite Goose Island’s own label promising it only “develops for up to 5 years in the bottle.” The Rodenbach Alexander from 2016 surprised me too, still tart and vinegary with a pleasing nuttiness, this was from a time when craft beer was still so exciting that I actually broke the release news for Esquire!

My interview had inspired Nyren, too. One night he cracked a long-cellared vertical of Brouwerij 3 Fonteinen Oude Geuze from the 2005 and 2008 “Nightlights” editions through the 2010, 2012, and 2014 vintages, the latter of which was still thankfully a standout.

“I had given up on ever drinking these and was trying to just sell ’em off until [it] summoned my old competitive collective OCD drinking spirit,” he joked.

Digging deep in my cellar one weekend, I found a small collection of BFM Abbaye de Saint Bon-Chien, a Swiss strong sour red ale aged in oak barrels. This was once, maybe, my favorite beer in the world, yet one I’d somehow forgotten I owned eight bottles of. The 2012 vintage brought it all flooding back, transportive as Proust’s madeleine, though not to a French childhood but to a decade ago, when people like me still cared about $40 bottles of sour Swiss beer.

Like Nyren, I was realizing I kind of missed our rare beer–drinking days, even if neither of us exactly wanted them back.

That crystallized one quiet Tuesday, when I pulled out an Against the Grain London Balling, a bourbon-barrel English barleywine from the Louisville brewery. If anything should survive a decade in the cellar it’s a barrel-aged barleywine, but this one was thin and hollow, barely there. What did come rushing back, however, was buying it back in 2012, on my first ever trip to Kentucky. That trip was where I first truly fell in love with bourbon, and where, without quite noticing, my main focus slowly began drifting from beer to whiskey.

And then I looked over at the shelves in my dining room. One floor above the beer cellar I no longer added to, out in the open where anyone could see, I’d spent the most recent decade building a still-growing collection of several hundred bottles of whiskey.

title: A Timeline of Craft Beer’s Darling Styles
summary:
Over the past 30 years or so, craft beer evolved from a semi-obscure curiosity to a known commodity. Perhaps more importantly, it’s made this journey without the sector ever fully selling out to the mainstream. Sure, several key brands were acquired by beer behemoths or made the leap into the realm of widespread distribution and popularity. But for the most part, craft beer’s engine still operates through the steady hum of smaller regional and cult brands pushing the beer scene forward through unique and innovative styles.

The article A Timeline of Craft Beer’s Darling Styles appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Over the past 30 years or so, craft beer evolved from a semi-obscure curiosity to a known commodity. Perhaps more importantly, it’s made this journey without the sector ever fully selling out to the mainstream. Sure, several key brands were acquired by beer behemoths or made the leap into the realm of widespread distribution and popularity. But for the most part, craft beer’s engine still operates through the steady hum of smaller regional and cult brands pushing the beer scene forward through unique and innovative styles.

At one point or another during these three decades, certain styles have bubbled up to the craft beer scene’s forefront as the industry’s darling brews. Sometimes their stars burn brightly before quickly fading. Occasionally, the “it” status gains a sense of anchoring permanency within the scene. There’s also the rare times when a style hatches its own subcategory of darlings, not unlike a beloved sitcom paving the way for successful spinoffs.

What follows is a rough timeline of the rise, fall, and occasional stability of these darling craft beer styles. While this roadmap naturally highlights a few obvious if not slightly ubiquitous types, it also features a few iterations that may not be recalled as easily. Of course, whether or not their flavor makes them worth recalling is relative.

1995 – 2000: American Pale Ale

American Pale Ale was the craft beer movement’s mother dough. It took some time for the public to warm up to the hoppy, fruity, more potent riff on traditional low-ABV English pales — the style’s flagship label, Sierra Nevada Pale Ale, was initially brewed in 1980. Once they did, though, obsession soon followed, arguably making it the first time people really nerded out over a specific beer style. It certainly wouldn’t be the last time: Labels like Dale’s Pale Ale from Oskar Blues Brewery and, yes, even the beers from the “it’s easy to forget they were a small craft brewery” beer titan Samuel Adams began pulling attention away from the heavyweights for doing things a little differently.

1995 – 2000: Hefeweizen

Brewed in Bavaria since the early 16th century — if not even earlier — Hefeweizen wasn’t a new category when it achieved darling status in the mid-’90s. But the easy-drinking wheat beer with the slightly cloudy composition was new to most American beer drinkers when pioneering breweries like Widmer Brothers and Pyramid began producing the style. While that perceived newness initially grabbed interest, its crisp, mildly fruity and phenolic flavors helped Hefeweizen retain top-level attention for nearly two decades.

1995 – 2000: Brown Ale

In retrospect, brown ale’s quick turn as craft beer’s “it” brew is slightly unorthodox, because the craft sector was only partially responsible for its popularity. Craft labels like Pete’s Wicked Ale were certainly instrumental in pushing the traditional British style to the top of the pedestal in the late ’90s, but so was the well-established British import Newcastle, which thrived in the States as it ironically plummeted in popularity back home. Both enticed plenty of folks to expand their sudsy horizons; sadly, the category’s starpower faded somewhat rapidly once people discovered more styles.

1995 – 2005: Amber Ale

For about 10 years, amber ale provided a crucial bridge between mainstream beers and more hardcore corners of the craft beer scene. The reason was fairly obvious. The subtly bittersweet style was darker than a lager and lighter than a stout, providing curious parties an approachable middle ground in both flavor and appearance that didn’t feel too esoteric. Much like brown ale, amber ale fell by the wayside when consumers were ready to be more adventurous.

1995 – 2005: West Coast IPA

The beloved brews of craft beer’s early years contained a sense of stylistic familiarity, even if hoppy characteristics like citrus and pine notes anchored their profile. The West Coast IPA trend shifted things dramatically, if not permanently. Bright and fruity yet also bitter and dank, West Coast IPA was an aggressive beer style in relation to what existed on the market at the time. With heavy hitting brands like Lagunitas and Stone Brewing, its market presence was just as aggressive as beer enthusiasts took heed. Over the years, other beers falling under the IPA umbrella would intrude on West Coast IPA’s popularity. However, its impact was so strong, it arguably remains the default way casual beer drinkers define the IPA category.

2000 – 2015: Double IPA/Extreme Beers

One of craft beer’s most notorious darlings essentially originated from an industry pissing contest. Around the turn of the century, breweries decided to push the limits of bitterness and alcohol. This resulted in intensely flavored, over-the-top hoppy styles like the double IPA. It also produced beers with higher ABVs than the average wine. They achieved darling status because people flocked to purchase them. Whether they bought them for their flavor or their novelty is an entirely different question.

2005 – 2015: American Belgian-Style/Farmhouse Ale

Belgian Trappist beer styles like Dubbel and Trippel built a cult following around the outset of the craft beer movement. While they were delicious, they weren’t sessionable because of their high-price point. Pioneering craft brewers like Allagash and Ommegang solved this problem by producing Belgian-style beers combining Belgian yeast strains with American ingredients. This offshoot not only gained mass appeal, it produced its own offshoot, the tart, earthy farmhouse ale. While they’re no longer the craft industry darling they once were, these unfussy beers still remain a solid retail presence.

2010 – 2015: Imperial Stout

By the end of the 2000s, Guinness was fully mainstream and stouts mostly shedded their status as an intimidating beer to most consumers. Imperial stouts reset this narrative by upping the intensity of classic stout notes. Unlike the increased bitterness of Double IPAs, this led to stronger notes of chocolate, coffee, and other pleasant treat-like notes. Enthusiasts championed the style, which would eventually spawn other popular and occasionally polarizing subgenres.

2010 – 2025: Niche IPA Substyles

IPAs just didn’t get extreme after the West Coast style became popular. They also got weird. A steady stream of IPA substyles started showing up at the beginning of the 2010s, when Black IPA’s odd juxtaposition of looking like a stout and tasting like an IPA bowled over craft hopheads. The ensuing IPA branches, such as the low-ABV Session IPA and the crisp, clean Cold IPA and Brut IPA, have been enthusiastically championed over the years, including some that almost feel like a mistake or even a dare now (we’re looking at you, Milkshake IPA).

2015 – Present: Barrel-Aged Beer

While craft beer produced a wide range of unique and innovative styles, it was still beer. Therefore, it was still a down-to-earth, approachable beverage. Then brewers started aging their beers in wine and spirits barrels anywhere from a couple of months to a couple of years. Suddenly, beer was fancy. Instead of scoffing at these elevated brews, craft beer enthusiasts stuck out their pinkies and embraced the trend with their full chest, even if these special brews left their wallet less than full. Today, barrel-aged beers’ combination of craftsmanship, unique flavor profile, and prestige continues to grant them darling status.

2015 – 2025: Hazy IPAs

Hazy IPAs did more than become an “it” beer in the mid-2010s. They changed the conversation around IPAs, and for the better. Cloudy, juicy, and low on bitterness, the beer enjoyed success for years as a regional cult brew along the East Coast, where they were known as New England IPAs, or NEIPAs. Word eventually got out; more importantly, so did pictures — part of the reason the style gained nationwide traction was because they looked good on Instagram. It remained a nationwide sensation because people found their brazen tropical notes to be a refreshing change from West Coast IPAs’ notorious bite.

2015 – 2020: Sours

Beer doesn’t always have to taste like beer. Sometimes, they can taste like mouth-puckering treats from your childhood. That may be the impetus behind why sours had their turn as a darling style. These tart, funky, and often vigorously fruit-forward brews brought existing styles like Lambics, Goses, and Berliner Weisses to the forefront of the craft scene, while also paving the way for newer substyles like the viscous, smoothie-like slushy beer. While the style is past peak popularity, they remain rather polarizing. Either you love it or you hate it, gray area be damned.

2015 – 2020: Pastry Stout

Stout styles imbued with sweet notes date back to the 19th century. The craft sector cranked this notion to 11 in the 2010s, as brewers keen on producing stout riffs turned their breweries into liquid bakeries, making brews featuring sweet culinary ingredients like cocoa nibs, vanilla beans, and coconut. The result was a decadent stout sub-category buoyed by beers which leaned into flavor notes typically associated with indulgent belt-loosening desserts like German chocolate cake, cookies, and gingerbread. Once the term “Pastry Stout” was coined in 2017, “it” status quickly followed, making the category the perfect yin to sour beer’s yang.

2020 – Present: Italian Pilsner

Right before Covid shut the world down, the craft scene started to drop hints that the next big thing was a return to basics. The surge in interest over Italian-style pilsners provided the first clue. There was nothing odd or esoteric about the style; craft breweries like Firestone Walker stuck to the formula of dry-hopping European hop varietals to produce crisp, subtly herbaceous brews with a subdued bitterness. It took a few years for the trend to take off — the most well-known version, Firestone Walker’s Pivo Pils, hit the market in 2012 — but once it did, there was no turning back.

2020 – Present: Mexican Lager

It’s entirely possible for a craft beer style to gain darling status because they’re simple and refreshing. That seems to be the case with Mexican lagers. Even if there’s something bigger behind the style’s initial surge, such as it being a symbolic post-Covid backlash to more esoteric styles, the crushable excellence of the crisp, flaked corn-kissed low-ABV brews doesn’t exactly hurt its still-unwavering popularity.

2025 – Present: Czech Lager

Coming off the heels of the Mexican lager trend, Czech lager’s current status as a craft darling feels as though the craft scene has come full circle. Like the early “it” beers in the craft sector, Czech-style lagers aren’t some wacky new innovation. They’re beer rooted in the traditions of classic Bohemian brewing techniques utilized since the mid-19th century. There’s no manipulations to amp bitterness, no fruit or chocolate finishes, no excess aging in an old Cabernet Sauvignon barrel. That doesn’t mean it’s totally bereft of innovation: The pristine foamy head produced when the Czech Lager comes from a Lukr faucet can make the beer look visually arresting. Aesthetics aside, thought, it’s just beer that tastes like beer, but in craft form. Sometimes, that’s all you can really ask for.

*Image retrieved from tito pixel via unsplash.com

title: We Asked 8 Chefs: What’s the One Dish You Never Order at a Restaurant?
summary:
More than other regular diners, chefs have a firsthand understanding of what goes on behind the scenes at restaurants. They know the dishes made with low-cost ingredients that are then highly marked up, the kinds of meals professional kitchens just can’t deliver on, and the typical days certain food orders come in. (Remember Anthony Bourdain’s infamous tip to not order fish at restaurants on Mondays because seafood orders tend to arrive on Tuesdays?) They also have specific palates. Cooks are constantly tasting the ingredients and dishes that go in and out of their kitchens.

The article We Asked 8 Chefs: What’s the One Dish You Never Order at a Restaurant? appeared first on VinePair.
content:
More than other regular diners, chefs have a firsthand understanding of what goes on behind the scenes at restaurants. They know the dishes made with low-cost ingredients that are then highly marked up, the kinds of meals professional kitchens just can’t deliver on, and the typical days certain food orders come in. (Remember Anthony Bourdain’s infamous tip to not order fish at restaurants on Mondays because seafood orders tend to arrive on Tuesdays?)

They also have specific palates. Cooks are constantly tasting the ingredients and dishes that go in and out of their kitchens. Always trying different flavors and textures helps cooks amass a uniquely keen palate.

All of these experiences inform what chefs do and, maybe more importantly, don’t order when they’re the ones dining out. But the everyday diner isn’t privy to such info. That’s why we asked eight chefs for the one dish they never order when at a restaurant. Read on to make sure you’re steering clear of these meals.

The dishes chefs never order at restaurants:

  • What the servers don’t recommend
  • Out-of-season vegetables
  • Gambas al ajillo
  • Pasta Alfredo
  • Overly complicated meals
  • Specials on a Monday
  • Liver
  • Andouillette
  • Nothing

“If there’s one dish I’ll never order at a restaurant, it’s the one the server isn’t enthusiastic about. I watch their expression when I ask, ‘Would you order this?’ If they hesitate, look unconvinced, or subtly steer me toward something else, I always take the hint. Your server knows — listen to them. Also, I love vegetables and am always excited to see seasonal produce on a menu, but if the vegetable sides feel thoughtlessly written, out of season, or included merely as an afterthought, I’ll never order them. A vegetarian dish shouldn’t feel like the token option; it deserves just as much creativity, intention, and care as everything else on the menu.” —Aarthi Sampath, chef and founder, Drāvida, New York City

“One dish I never order at a restaurant is gambas al ajillo. Traditionally, the dish is very simple — made with small rock shrimp, quality olive oil, paper-thin sliced garlic, and cayenne pepper — allowing the quality of the main ingredients to truly shine. However, the variations I often see served in the U.S. stray too far from the authentic version, which takes away from what makes the dish special.” —Rafa de la Rosa, sous chef, Minetta Tavern, and executive chef consultant, Techo Palma, Washington, D.C.

“When I go out to an Italian restaurant, one dish I never order is pasta Alfredo. Cream sauces are very filling, and with Alfredo, every bite tends to taste exactly the same to me. I prefer dishes where the flavors and textures change from forkful to forkful, which makes the experience more interesting and enjoyable.” —Glenn Rolnick, director of culinary operations, Carmine’s Italian Restaurant, NYC

“I’m going to scrub the menu and find the simplest item they serve. I tend to avoid anything that sounds overly complicated because, in my experience, it can become contrived and convoluted — overthought and ultimately fall flat. I want something that showcases how a few premium components can elevate a dish to unexpected heights. That tells me the chef and their kitchen know how to perform. As chefs, we’re conduits and facilitators, not the story itself. Let the food shine and leave the ego behind.” —Chris Meier, executive chef, The Curtis, Denver

“I think it always pays off to listen to your server. I don’t like to ask a server their favorite item because that’s so subjective, but I do often ask what a server recommends. If I ever hear a server say ‘you can order it,’ or ‘it’s not my favorite but people like it,’ then I generally take that as a little helpful warning to avoid the dish.” —Chris McLaurin, chef, Lutra Cafe & Bakery, Durham, N.C.

“I will never order specials on Mondays because they are often leftovers from the weekend. I really love to eat everything, but if I see any kind of liver on the menu, such as chicken liver pate or calf liver, I will not order it because my grandmother used to feed it to me all the time when I was a child.” —Carlos Barroz, executive chef and partner, Palermo Argentinian Bistro, NYC

“Once, when I was in college, I was traveling through Lyon, France. I was eating dinner in a small brasserie near the train station. I saw “andouillette” on the menu. Thinking it was andouille sausage I ordered it. It turns out andouillette is a sausage stuffed with stomach and intestine. The most prized andouillette gets its pungency from the colon. It’s definitely something I won’t order again.” —Brian Rae, culinary director, ES Hospitality, Boston

“As a chef and restaurateur, I would never single out a certain dish that I wouldn’t order! You’d be surprised how often the most banal item on a menu can be the best thing happening in a kitchen. A wedge salad, the chicken dish, the sweetbreads — all can change your life if done right. If you immediately say no, how would you ever know if you’re limiting yourself?” —Erik Niel, chef and owner, Easy Bistro & Bar, Main Street Meats, and Little Coyote, Chattanooga, Tenn.
